title: The word heard first in the yard at Muileann chaol
summary: A carrier bringing salt fish to the Library's kitchen uses the word seann-chunntas in the yard within Sìleas nic Rath's hearing; she copies it into her working notes, meaning at first only to ask Raghnall whether the Library's glossary should carry it.

title: Ellen Marsh's letter carries the word twice
summary: A civil note from Ellen Marsh asking after the eleventh book's binding uses seann-chunntas twice in passing, as a word already in general currency in the north; Sìleas sets it beside the carrier's yard-talk and begins to understand what the word joins.

title: Sìleas enters the word without a heading
summary: Sìleas nic Rath sets a single line at the foot of a Board return, noting the word heard that year joining the tabled request and the dead motion, and that no Dia-thìreach in office has yet used it; she gives it no category of its own.

title: The Board's order to Achadh dhomhain
summary: A four-line order from the Mine Board reaches the maor of Achadh dhomhain in an Gearran, closing the Sloc Mòr's upper galleries and the timbering left to stand, the shafts capped, the workings judged to cost more in pumping than the coal they still gave.

title: One face given to the Rite
summary: The deepest and driest of the Sloc Mòr's old workings is kept open, given whole to the houses of Brìde's order to cut altar-coal, a few baskets a year, no more than the Rite's own accounting requires.

title: The twelve sworn at Achadh dhomhain
summary: A priest sent from the southern Seann Skell swears twelve hewers to cut the altar-face, using an oath drawn from the dissolved Guild of Hewers' own rolls; among them an old man who had sworn the guild's oath as a young hewer, near sixty years before.

title: The maor's report on the hewing families
summary: The maor of Achadh dhomhain reports that the old hewing families of the town said nothing against the closing of the Sloc Mòr's upper galleries and asked nothing of the Board in its place.

title: The regiments' fighters at the Còmhrag
summary: Each of the nine regiments sends a fighter to the yearly melee at Ceann leathan for the first time; the ninth regiment's man, once a fitter under Peigi nic Ascaill's own charter, wins it in the third bout, and the crowd cheers him no louder than any winner before the war.

title: The second regiment's guard at the Library's gate
summary: Six men of the second regiment pitch a tent in the Library's own yard and stand a guard at its gate over the sealed room; Raghnall mac Mhuirich watches the first of them arrive from his window on the morning they come.

title: Raghnall's letter that got no answer
summary: Raghnall writes to the council that the Library never asked for a guard and has never needed one to keep a room its own lock already held shut, and asks the council's reasons; none come that year or the next.

title: Eachann given the last coal run
summary: The yard masters at Muileann chrom tell Eachann mac Ruairidh, three days before, that the run he is given will be the coal line's last working under coal's own name, an old lamp-house contract closing after fourteen years of the line carrying dubhan under the unchanged name.

title: The last coal train reaches Cathair dhearg
summary: On 10 an t-Sultain Eachann mac Ruairidh brings six wagons of coal down from Achadh dhomhain to the capital's goods-yard, unshunting them himself; a knot of yard hands and old drivers gathers along the platform with no cheer and no speech, only raised hands and a single nod.

title: The coal handed to carters, not a second engine
summary: The lamp-houses judge six wagons not worth a second engine's steam and carry the last coal on by horse and cart from the goods-yard, so that the trade which crowned the kingdom's kings goes out under its own name behind horses at the last.

title: The first pass shown at the boundary stones
summary: The sixth regiment sets a table in the shadow of the northern boundary stones and begins issuing printed passes; for the first time since the Severance a Tuathach going south past the stones must show one, the council's minute calling it a measure for a time only.

title: Sìleas copies the council's three words
summary: Sìleas nic Rath enters the council's minute on the northern passes exactly as given, for a time only, the same three words the wartime tithe was given six years before and has not since been taken away.

title: Tuathaich wool sold on its northern day
summary: At the fair at Muileann òg, Tuathaich wool is sold on its own northern day through Dia-thìrich factors as it has been sold since the first fair after the truce; Ùna nic Ailein's court enters the day's takings in the ordinary column.

title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh dies at Àth dhìreach
summary: A letter in the hand of Beathag's own sister brings word that Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh has died quietly in the night at her sister's house at Àth dhìreach, five-and-seventy years old, six years after laying down the chronicler's office.

title: Sìleas writes the one entry the day requires
summary: Sìleas nic Rath enters Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's death in the open chronicle in the plain accounting the office requires, naming her the first hand to note the fuel and the re-header of fourteen years, and adds nothing of grief beyond it.

title: An old hewer sworn a second time
summary: At the swearing of the Rite's twelve hewers at Achadh dhomhain an old man who had sworn the guild's oath in his youth tells the priest he had thought it the last oath a coal-cutter's trade would ask of him.

title: The Sloc Mòr's upper galleries capped
summary: Within a fortnight of the Board's order the eleven upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr are capped, their timbering left standing in the dark.

title: The ninth regiment's man at Ceann leathan
summary: The winner of the Còmhrag in the regiments' first year is a broad Dia-thìreach of the southern Seann Skell who had fitted engines under the Fuel-Fitters' charter before the regiments took him.

title: A sentry's word at the Library gate
summary: The sergeant of the second regiment's first watch at an Leabharlann tells the keeper it is a queer sort of soldiering, standing watch over a door that has never opened from either side.

title: The last coal carter of the north road
summary: The last carter to bring coal down the north road past An Taigh-seinnse Reòta above Muileann fhada carries a load of small coal for the landlord's own kitchen and none for sale.

title: Achadh mhòr's harvest in the present
summary: The harvest of Achadh mhòr goes down to the capital in the Board's lorries and the growers' own; the factors reckon it the heaviest in a generation and the dearest to carry.

title: The eighth regiment at Inis uaine keeps a school
summary: The eighth regiment at Inis uaine keeps a school in its barracks for the soldiers' children and the town's, taught by a corporal who had been a copyist.
